newsitem.title: HONDURAS: Ex-Haiti police chief denies drugs charges.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Haiti police chief denies drugs charges.

text.p: Exiled Haitian strongman Lt. Col. Joseph Michel Francois, now under arrest in Honduras pending extradition to Miami, denied on Monday he was a central figure in a huge drugs smuggling network.

"I am innocent of the charges they are accusing me of. How many times do I have to say I know nothing about drugs," he told reporters at the Central Penitentiary in the Honduran capital Tegucigalpa, where is being held prior to travelling under escort to the United States.

An indictment unveiled in a Miami court on Friday said Francois, the former police chief of Port-au-Prince, put the security network of Haiti's 1991-94 military government under his control to ship thousands of kilos of cocaine and heroin into the United States in league with Colombian drugs cartels.

Francois, who is also believed to have been the mastermind behind the 1991 coup that toppled President Jean-Bertrand Aristide, was arrested on Friday by Honduran police in San Pedro Sula, 165 kms (100 miles) north of Tegucigalpa.
U.S. law enforcement officials in Miami were hoping he would be brought to the United States by late Monday.

Francois said he had been targeted by Washington in "revenge" for not heeding its demands that he leave Haiti and hand power back to Aristide. He said he did not regret taking part in the 1991 coup because otherwise the government would have killed him.

He fled to the Dominican Republic in 1994 after U.S. troops occupied the Caribbean nation to restore Aristide to power. He was given asylum in Honduras a year ago when Dominican authorities arrested him on charges of plotting to overthrow the Haitian government again.
In San Pedro Sula, Francois, who is alleged to have made millions of dollars from deals with the Colombian cartels, set up a business selling furniture and domestic appliances.

He became the Port-au-Prince police chief after the 1991 coup and developed a network of plainclothes policemen, or "attaches", who instigated a reign of terror against opponents of the military regime.
The U.S. indictment said his drug network operated from June 1987 until about September last year, and moved 33 tonnes of drugs into the United States.
